sections.title: 1. The Customer Problem and Discovery
sections.text: 1. The Customer Problem and DiscoveryFrom Feature Request to Customer Outcome Here is the ask: a single process has to drive a document sign-off, a payment, an email and updates in three in-house systems. Any one of those steps may break, or may sit idle for days. The people around the table want different things from day one: The business sponsor wants every case to reach the end. The operations lead asks for retries, a clear view of each case and a way to roll back. The application team does not want yet another fragile web of direct integrations. The auditor needs proof of each approval: who gave it, at what time and under which control. Resist naming a tool first. Put the problem into a single sentence that does not yet pick a product. A weak, feature-led version: "Let's build an orchestrator that calls the payment, email and three internal APIs". It is accurate, yet it puts the wiring ahead of the result the customer wants. A strong, outcome-led version: "apply each business effect of a long-running process exactly once, keep its state visible, and compensate when a step fails." That one line already demands idempotency, durable state, retries, pauses for human approval, auditability and compensating actions. It also names the job: guarding a business transaction spread over days, rather than a stream of messages. Framing it like this shows the habit panels hire FDEs (Forward Deployed Engineers) for: you take vague customer words and turn them into a goal you can measure. Stakeholder Map and Jobs-to-Be-Done Group the four stakeholder sets by the job each needs done, not by title. Lump them together and you will optimise the wrong part of the system. Workflow participants: they need to "look at a case and decide, with the full context in front of them." Operations teams: they need to "spot stuck cases, learn the cause and bring each one back safely." Application developers: they need to "connect a system once, without writing bespoke retry code for every corner case." Auditors: they need to "rebuild the trail of decisions and check that each control held." Reliability means something different to each. Participants want clarity. Operators want to recover cases without crossing integration boundaries. Auditors want a trail they can follow. A strong answer meets every group's need, and no single group gets to steer the whole design. The Two-Minute Opening Answer An opening you could say out loud in the room: "So we have a document sign-off, a payment, an email and three in-house systems to coordinate, and each step might fail or stall for days. First I'd pin down whose workflow this is, which business event counts as done, and which steps need a person to approve and which run on their own. My working goal: apply each business effect of a long-running process exactly once, keep its state visible, and compensate when a step fails. Unless you say otherwise, I'll take durable state, retries, an audit history and recovery from worker crashes as given. Next I'd size the volume, the latency and how much failure we can absorb. Then I'd build the orchestration, security and observability on top of those numbers." In under two minutes that opening repeats the ask, names who it serves, sets the goal and flags each assumption where facts are missing. Under time pressure, compress by asking fewer questions and making each one count. Highest-Leverage Discovery Questions You do not need equal depth on every subsystem. Pick the questions that remove the most doubt per minute. Clarify the business finish line: Which event tells us the workflow is done? Do we count success when every technical step finishes, or when the business effect lands exactly once? For each kind of failure, do we roll back or compensate? Identify the workflow shape: Does it run with no humans, with a person in the loop, or a blend? Which steps may pause for minutes, which for hours and which for days? Can a case fork, loop back to an earlier step or get cancelled halfway? Determine blast radius and ownership: Which team owns each internal integration? Whose pager goes off when a case stalls? Who has the authority to resume, rerun or override a case? Pin down trust and compliance requirements: Which evidence must we keep for audit? Which actions need an approval log or a signature trail? Do residency, retention or data-minimisation rules apply? When the interviewer holds facts back, say that openly and record the gap as an assumption. For example: "I can't tell yet if payment is the final business effect or only one link in a longer approval chain. So I'll treat a payment retry as safe only when the provider honours idempotency keys and a durable workflow record proves the effect landed once." The Assumption Ledger Think of the assumption ledger as a running list of things you treat as true until the customer says otherwise. Every entry worth writing has four fields: Assumption: the belief you are acting on for now Impact: how the design changes if it holds or fails Verification: the step that would confirm it Owner or follow-up: the person who can answer, or the deadline for an answer First example: Assumption: the payment provider accepts idempotency keys Impact: decides if a retry can run without charging twice Verification: check the provider docs or ask whoever owns payments Owner or follow-up: the payment integration team, before the design is final Second example: Assumption: participants can live with a pause of several days Impact: shapes how long state is kept, when cases expire and how people get notified Verification: check with the business sponsor and the support team Owner or follow-up: the product owner, ahead of any sizing work Every discovery blends confirmed facts with provisional guesses. A guess nobody writes down quietly turns into a design decision. In an interview, splitting checked requirements from assumptions often earns more credit than naming a particular product. Interview pointer: Panels like to test whether your discovery stays honest when the clock is running. Keep the four-field ledger (assumption, impact, verification, owner) ready to use. It shows rigour and costs you almost no time. Turning Discovery into Scope, Risks, and Success Discovery is where the system gets its shape, so treat it as real design work. When it ends, you should hold four outputs, in your head or on the whiteboard: Scope: the workflows we will handle and the ones we will not Assumptions: the beliefs we act on until someone confirms them Risks: the places where duplicates, lost data or unauthorised actions could creep in Owners: the named owner of every integration, approval, escalation and support route Describe success the way the business would, not the way infrastructure would. Skip "messages processed" and "tasks retried". Measure the count of completed workflows. Add the duplicate-prevention rate, the compensation success rate and the mean time to detect stuck cases. Also check that an operator can walk through any case from its first step to its last. A success test small enough for an interview: the business effect landed once, the user sees where the case stands, and each exception leads to a known compensation or escalation. Stakeholder Map in Practice Take a concrete case. A contract gets approved, a payment fires, an email goes out and three internal systems get updated. The end user is a real person waiting for an approval or a payout. It is not "the API". The operator is whoever is on call when a worker dies just after the payment went through. The security owner rules on who may resume or override a stuck case. The executive sponsor wants a process that behaves predictably, passes compliance and never has to be pieced back together from spreadsheets. Again, the aim is to serve all four groups while none of them takes over the design. The Interview Signal Hiring Teams Listen For Panels check more than your diagrams. They watch whether you can go from a customer's pain to a concrete technical design without sliding into vague platform talk. The best candidates make the problem specific. They name the people, state their assumptions out loud and describe success in words the customer would use. Draw the architecture only once you can say whose workflow is changing and how success gets measured. Before that point, you are listing software features, not designing a system the business can rely on.

sections.title: 2. Clarifying Questions, Requirements, and Constraints
sections.text: 2. Clarifying Questions, Requirements, and ConstraintsChoosing Which Unknowns to Pay For Skip the boxes and arrows at first. Start by picking which open questions deserve scarce interview time. Expect the interviewer to answer only some of what you ask. Strong candidates live with some ambiguity and instead: Find the handful of choices that would reshape the design if they went the other way. Guard the riskiest constraint first: no business effect may happen twice when a step fails, pauses, or comes back in the wrong order. The Question Tree for Discovery Keep discovery questions few and pointed, each tied to a concrete design choice: In what order do the steps run, and can any of them branch or be skipped? → The answer tells you if a simple sequential runner will do, or if you need a real state machine. Which steps can be undone after they succeed, and which cannot? → This marks where compensation is safe and where retries need extra caution. What is the longest a workflow may stay open before it times out, gets archived or is cancelled? → Storage and timers follow from this; week-long waits rule out in-memory state and short-lived queues. At what point does a person approve, and how long may that approval sit? → This drives how you model paused states, reminders, escalations and cases nobody comes back to. Do the downstream systems accept idempotency keys, block replays, or take a unique business reference? → If yes, retries are safe; if not, the orchestrator has to wrap each call in its own deduplication layer. If a definition changes mid-flight, how do older running instances stay compatible? → This bites the moment someone wants a new approval step while 10,000 old workflows are live. Partial answers are no reason to stall. State your assumptions out loud and tie each one to the risk it covers. The safest anchor here is that payment is the riskiest step and cannot be reversed. Whatever else degrades, the design must still block a second payment. From Discovery to Requirements Turn what you learned into a ranked list, not a wish list, sorted into must, should and could: Must: durable state machine, persisted transition history, idempotent activity execution, retry and timeout policies, human signals and timers, saga compensation, operator recovery. Should: versioned workflow definitions, so running instances can evolve without breaking. Could: deeper analytics, bespoke dashboards, or branching rules users configure themselves, as long as none of them puts correctness at risk. The reason behind each must-have: Durable state machine: the workflow outlives a crashed process and waits out long pauses. Persisted transition history: operators can see what happened, and a restarted worker recovers its intent from the record instead of guessing. Idempotent activity execution: retries will happen. A retry with no deduplication is a duplicate side effect under a nicer name. Retry and timeout policies: outside systems break, slow down, and sometimes stay silent forever. Human signals and timers: an approval usually arrives as a business event, not as an API callback. Saga compensation and operator recovery: some steps can be reversed and some cannot, and the design has to show which is which. sections.text: 3. Scale Estimates, SLOs, and CapacityStart with the Load That Breaks the First Draft Most candidates open with a sensible sketch: a workflow service, a queue, a pool of workers, a state database and a blob store for attachments. At average load, it holds up. Its weak spot is timing as much as volume. Long waits, retries and deadline pressure stack up, and that mix is the limit the sketch hides. Picture a workflow that idles for days. Then approvals arrive, a payment gateway answers, or a downstream system recovers, and the work spikes at once. A system sized for the mean will miss business deadlines once it is live. So estimate the envelope next. Count the workflows running at the same time and the events they emit. Work out how much state needs durable retention, how fast tasks must go out, and how much slack peaks and partial outages call for. Working Assumptions and Activity Rate Treat the scenario figures as planning inputs, not fixed truth: 10 million active workflows 100 million activities per day Week-long waits between some steps Those figures describe a durable state machine. Most of its population sits idle, while a smaller slice keeps moving. Turn the daily figure into a rate: 100,000,000 activities/day ÷ 86,400 seconds/day ≈ 1,157 activities/second on average. The mean is a useful anchor, but you do not provision for it. Real peaks can land several times higher. Work bunches up in office hours. Reminders go out in a morning batch. A dependency outage holds retries back, then releases them together. Say the framing out loud. These multipliers are my own planning choices for this case, and I'd defend them; they are not industry standards: Average dispatch rate: roughly 1.2k activities/sec Peak dispatch rate: 3x–10x average, set by how the customer uses the system Headroom: for a new system, at least double the observed peak; go higher still if regional failover or retries matter Growth factor: run the numbers at both 2x and 10x future scale before you fix partition counts or storage layout Separate Workflow State from Payloads A frequent scaling error is to push everything into the workflow history. Keep durable state small. It needs only the facts that let you replay, resume, audit and compensate: version markers, step status, timestamps, business references and correlation IDs. Big items go elsewhere. Documents, PDFs, images and payloads from internal systems live in object storage or a document store, and the workflow keeps a pointer. The split pays off in three ways: Replay cost: if every retry or rehydration drags megabytes of payload into the orchestration engine, latency climbs and worker memory comes under strain. Retention cost: audit and support often need workflow histories kept for a long time. Park large payloads on the hot path and the operational ledger becomes a costly archive. Blast radius: when every event record carries its own copy of the payload, a leak or an accidental change does far more harm. As a rule, workflow state holds only enough to keep the system deterministic and inspectable. Payload storage takes the data that is large, mutable or sourced from outside. The workflow points at the payload; it never turns into it. Estimating Event-History Storage Estimate it with a quick product: active workflows × events retained per workflow × bytes per event. Inputs (10 million is the scenario's figure; the per-workflow numbers are my own): 10 million active workflows An average of 40 retained events per workflow 1 KB per event record (an illustrative size) The result is about 400 GB of raw event data. That leaves out replication, indexing, compaction overhead and backups. If each event takes 2 KB rather than 1 KB, the total grows to about 800 GB. If the true active set is 20 million, not 10 million, the figure doubles once more. The estimate shows which dimension drives the storage design. It is not a final figure. When history is kept for a long time, give the colder audit path its own home, apart from the hot execution path that holds task leases and execution metadata. Compaction, tiering and retention policies then become simpler to think through. Estimating Task-Queue Throughput The task queue is where operations choke. Every status update, payment request, internal API call and approval notification ends up as a queued task. At 100M activities/day, the system has to accept, lease and complete a sustained flow above ~1,157 activities/second. That figure still hides load. Each activity usually triggers at least two queue actions, an enqueue and a dequeue. Leasing, visibility timeouts and requeues can add more. So the throughput envelope covers both creating tasks and running them: Task enqueues: grow roughly in line with activity count Task leases and acknowledgements: one or more per activity, often extra once retries kick in Retry traffic: added load after transient failures or worker restarts The queue subsystem must survive a retry storm and still serve new tasks. A practical design splits queues by priority class, workflow type or workflow tenant. Then no single customer, and no runaway workflow family, can monopolise dispatch capacity. Sensitivity at 10x Growth A sensitivity table makes the scaling decision concrete. It shows what gives way first when the assumptions shift: Scenario Active workflows Activities/day Avg activities/sec Likely architectural pressure Base case 10M 100M ~1.2k Durable history, a moderate degree of partitioning, a worker pool kept warm 10x growth 100M 1B ~11.6k More aggressive sharding, tighter isolation between queues, heavier compaction and tiering At 10x, I would not expect application-server CPU to give out first. I'd expect replay latency, hot spots in the queue, storage fan-out or operating cost to hit the wall sooner. If the design would need a full rewrite to take that growth, say so. Then pick a layout that partitions more easily from day one. Latency Budgets and Workflow SLOs Workflow orchestration needs a different set of SLIs/SLOs from a typical API server: Availability SLI (service level indicator): the share of time that workflow submission, progress updates and operator controls can be reached Latency SLI: how long it takes to accept a new step, send out an activity, and show a state change in the UI Freshness SLI: the lag between a real-world event and its appearance in workflow state Quality SLI: the rate of stuck workflows, failed compensations, missed transitions or duplicate side effects Security SLI: the fraction of requests that pass authorisation correctly and get audited; the rate of sensitive-data exposure is pushed toward zero by design, never claimed to be impossible Cost SLI: cost per workflow or per thousand activities, plus the support effort that operator intervention demands Turn these into objectives the customer can feel. Few customers care whether a task lease takes 80ms or 120ms. They do care when a payment step shows up in the UI so late that an operator thinks it was lost and retries it by hand. They also care when a workflow that ought to be compensating stays hidden for hours. Size the queue subsystem to ride out a retry storm with new tasks still flowing. Partitioning by tenant, workflow type or priority class stops one runaway workflow family from monopolising dispatch capacity. Retry Math Is Not Compensation This formula puts a bound on repeat attempts and avoids a thundering herd: backoff_n = min(cap, base × 2^n) + jitter Here n is the retry attempt number, base is the first delay, cap is the longest allowed delay, and jitter is randomised variation so retries do not fire in sync. Exponential backoff spaces out attempts after a failure. That shields dependencies and gives a transient incident room to clear. Backoff is not business compensation: The payment goes through but the email fails. Retrying the email is the right move. The payment goes through, and later the workflow finds a validation error. Backoff cannot reverse the charge. You need an explicit compensation step, such as a refund or marking the case for review. Retry says "try once more, later". Compensation asks "which business action reverses or limits a side effect that already happened?" Keep the two apart. Treat cap and jitter as operational trade-offs tied to the business process, never as habits: A low cap recovers user-facing work faster, but it can swamp a flaky dependency. A high cap protects the dependency, but customers wait longer to see progress. Interview pointer: Interviewers like to set the "retry vs. compensation" trap. Say plainly that backoff never stands in for a business-level reversal, such as a refund, when a side effect that already completed has to be undone. Which Estimate Should Drive the Architecture Total workflow count alone rarely decides it. The mix of long waits, visible state and safe side effects does: Week-long waits demand durable storage and the ability to replay. 100 million daily activities demand a scalable queue and a partition strategy. Side effects you cannot undo demand compensation tooling, unique business keys and idempotency. Let the stress point choose the components, not whatever is easiest to sketch: When history volume is the main load → tune storage tiering and retention policies. When the dispatch rate leads → invest in queue partitioning and worker elasticity. When external APIs are the pressure → work on retries, circuit breaking and throttles per integration. When manual recovery takes the most effort → improve observability, the operator UI and audit trails. Communicating Uncertainty Like an Operator Interviewers look for proof that you steer with estimates, rather than pretend to be certain. A sample answer: "I'd take 10 million active workflows as the starting working set. But I'd plan partitions and queue namespaces for a 10x sensitivity case, since growth and retry bursts rarely spread load evenly. If the customer later says only 20% of workflows run long, storage gets simpler. If they say 80% have week-long waits, retention and the replay path jump to the top of my list." That answer shows you picking the smallest design that stays safe under realistic growth and failure. You are not over-building for every future you can dream up. This topic sorts candidates. Plenty of engineers can talk about distributed systems in the abstract. Fewer can name the number that matters, explain why, and say which decision it moves. Treat estimates as tools for decisions. Each number should back an architectural choice or an operational limit. If a metric leaves partitioning, storage, retry policy, latency budget and support model all unchanged, it probably does not belong at the front of your answer.

sections.text: 4. Architecture and End-to-End FlowSystem Boundary and Customer Outcome Start with what the customer needs and design back from it. The outcome: apply each business effect of a long-running process exactly once, keep its state visible, and compensate when a step fails. Retries still happen. "Exactly once" means nobody is charged twice or sent the same message twice, no step goes missing unnoticed, and you can show all of that. Component Map: Control Plane vs Data Plane Draw a line between the control plane and the data plane before anything else. Without it, the parts never fall into place. Components: Workflow definition registry: holds the approved workflow templates. It is the source of truth for their step order, their retry and timeout rules, and which compensation undoes which step. Durable history store: the system of record. It logs every attempt, signal, state transition, receipt and final outcome. Workflow scheduler: derives the next runnable transition from durable history and hands it off to run. Activity task queues: buffer the handoff from scheduler decisions to the workers. Workers: make external calls, apply internal side effects and run local validation. Timer service: brings a workflow back after a delay, at a deadline, or when a human wait ends. Signal/approval gateway: takes explicit signals from people or systems and releases the workflow waiting on them. Compensation engine: after a terminal failure, runs business actions that undo, as far as they can, the steps already finished. Operations UI: shows live state, who is blocking whom, and the retry history, with pause, resume and override controls. System Boundary and Customer Outcome

    • Workflow scheduler: derives the next runnable transition from durable history and hands it off to run.
    • Activity task queues: buffer the handoff from scheduler decisions to the workers.

    • Timer service: brings a workflow back after a delay, at a deadline, or when a human wait ends.

sections.text: 5. Data Model, APIs, and Working CodeThe Smallest Safe Slice of the System Boxes on a whiteboard don't convince an interviewer. Durable records, strict contracts and one code path that runs the riskiest part safely do. Here the riskiest part is the state machine. It picks the next move once a step has succeeded, failed or been replayed. The approval screen and email sender matter far less. Get the state machine wrong and the customer suffers, however healthy the rest is: cards charged twice, lost approvals, workflows that look frozen for good. Core Durable Records Four records carry the design. Give each a purpose, a key, a lifecycle and a retention rule: WorkflowInstance(id, definition_version, state, next_event): the single row that owns one business process. Purpose: the one durable record of where the workflow stands and where it will resume. Primary key: id. Lifecycle: created at start, changed on each transition, and finally archived or kept as the customer's policy requires. Retention: hold the live row while the workflow runs. Once it finishes, keep a slimmer historical copy if audit or replay needs one. HistoryEvent(instance_id, sequence, type, payload_ref): an audit trail you only ever add to. Purpose: rebuild the exact order of events without leaning on memory or short-lived logs. Primary key: (instance_id, sequence). Lifecycle: new events get appended; past events are never edited. Retention: keep events while debugging, customer audits and replay still need them. After that, policy moves them to cold storage or deletes them. ActivityReceipt(idempotency_key, external_ref, status): a note of each side effect that has been tried or has finished. Purpose: stop a retry from taking payment again, sending a second email or repeating an update. Primary key: idempotency_key. Lifecycle: written just before or just after the external effect, depending on how the dependency behaves. Retention: keep it for as long as duplicates must be blocked. Timer(instance_id, fire_at): a record of each scheduled wake-up. Purpose: wake a workflow after a long wait, expire an approval, or check whether an outside job has finished. Primary key: (instance_id, fire_at), or whatever key the scheduler uses instead. Lifecycle: insert it when a wait starts and delete it once the wait ends. Insert it again if the workflow is retried. Ownership is split. The orchestrator holds workflow state, the history of steps and the intent to retry. Payments, document approval, email delivery and CRM (customer relationship management) updates belong to external systems. The orchestrator may record a payment, but it never acts as the financial ledger. API Contracts Four API contracts expose the state machine. Each is quick to explain, yet strict enough that no client can slip vague work into the engine: POST /v1/workflows/{type}: begins a new workflow. Authentication: normal caller authentication, scoped to the tenant or customer. Idempotency: the caller sends an idempotency key, so a retried call never yields a second instance. Request: the workflow type, the business payload, caller context and, if wanted, correlation metadata. Response: the instance id, the starting state and a status reference that does not change. Errors: 400 for a malformed request; 401/403 when auth fails; 409 while a request with that key is still in flight; 422 when the key returns with a different payload, or the inputs make no business sense. This split of 409 and 422 comes from the IETF Idempotency-Key draft, which had expired by Sep 2026: an Internet-Draft, not an RFC. POST /v1/workflows/{id}/signals: accepts input from a person or another system. Authentication: the caller needs permission to signal this workflow or tenant. Idempotency: a signal id combined with a payload hash, or a caller key, filters out double-clicked approvals and repeated system callbacks. Response: the accepted signal and the transition it caused, or a no-op when that signal has already been applied. GET /v1/workflows/{id}/history: returns the audit trail. Authentication: the caller needs read rights for the workflow's tenant and policy scope. Semantics: it never writes; results come back in pages, sorted by sequence. Errors: 404 when the workflow does not exist; 403 when access policy hides it. POST /v1/workflows/{id}/repair: gives operators, or automation they have approved, a way to resume, replay or compensate. Authentication: elevated operator authorisation with a narrow scope. Idempotency: each repair action carries its own idempotency token. An operator who clicks twice should not cause twice the side effects. Semantics: the call must state plainly which action it takes: retry a step, compensate a finished step, or resume from a known checkpoint. Duplicates should behave predictably. If the payment step sees one idempotency key twice, the first call takes the money and saves a receipt. The second returns that receipt, or a "completed already" response. The Implementation Slice That Proves the Design One saga step is enough to show the key behaviour: wait for approval, take payment idempotently, update the CRM, and compensate if a downstream step fails for good. The sketch is narrow by design. Production code would also need a scheduler, queue workers, persistence, serialisation, distributed locking and stronger typing. Here we keep only the state transitions an interviewer cares about most. from dataclasses import dataclass from typing import Protocol class PermanentError(Exception): pass @dataclass(frozen=True) class Order: id: str amount_cents: int customer_email: str @dataclass(frozen=True) class PaymentReceipt: idempotency_key: str external_ref: str status: str class Activities(Protocol): async def charge(self, order: Order, idempotency_key: str) -> PaymentReceipt: ... async def update_crm(self, order: Order, idempotency_key: str) -> None: ... async def send_receipt(self, order: Order, idempotency_key: str) -> None: ... async def refund(self, payment: PaymentReceipt, idempotency_key: str) -> None: ... async def order_workflow(order: Order, activities: Activities, wait_for_approval): if order.amount_cents <= 0: raise ValueError("order amount must be positive") approved = await wait_for_approval(order.id, timeout_days=7) if not approved: return "rejected" payment_key = f"pay:{order.id}" payment = await activities.charge(order, idempotency_key=payment_key) try: await activities.update_crm(order, idempotency_key=f"crm:{order.id}") await activities.send_receipt(order, idempotency_key=f"mail:{order.id}") except PermanentError: await activities.refund(payment, idempotency_key=f"refund:{order.id}") raise return "completed" What each part does, in an order you can talk through out loud: Order and PaymentReceipt are typed objects at the boundary. They stop the orchestration code from passing loose blobs around. PermanentError separates failures worth a business retry from failures that should start compensation. Activities is a protocol rather than a concrete dependency. That makes it easy to test, and it keeps vendor SDK details out of the workflow logic. order_workflow(...) coordinates the saga. The opening check turns away plainly bad input before any side effect. It is typed validation at the workflow's edge. Waiting for approval creates a pause that must survive restarts. In production, a timer and stored state back it, not a bare function call. payment_key = f"pay:{order.id}" guards the charge. A retry, a worker crash or a redelivered message cannot trigger a second one. activities.charge(...) touches the outside world. The orchestrator reads its return value as a receipt; the payment ledger remains the source of truth. After payment, the saga moves on to update_crm(...) and then send_receipt(...). except PermanentError compensates by issuing a refund. Raising the error again keeps the failure visible. The orchestrator can then record the terminal state and show it in history. Interview pointer: Expect a question on how fine-grained the idempotency keys are, and answer it head-on. Each business action with a side effect gets its own key (pay:, crm:, mail:, refund:). The workflow as a whole does not share one. That single detail moves an answer from a whiteboard sketch to something a team could run in production. What the Whiteboard Version Omits on Purpose The short snippet leaves out concurrency control, versioning and observability hooks. A real build needs all of them: Optimistic concurrency: each WorkflowInstance update checks a version number, so two workers cannot both move the same instance forward from stale state. In practice: "update where version = expected_version"; if another worker got there first, retry or abort. Schema and contract versioning: definition_version on the instance lets old and new definitions run at the same time. An instance in flight stays on the version it began with, unless an explicit migration policy says otherwise. Idempotency at every write boundary: payment is only one case. Repair actions, email sends, CRM updates and approval signals should be as safe to replay, where that is feasible. Observability: every transition should produce metrics, trace spans and structured logs, tagged with step name, outcome and instance_id. The history table is the system of record. Telemetry is there for fast diagnosis. Policy checks around model output: an LLM (large language model) might classify, route or summarise work inside a step. Before that output can change state or fire an external action, it must clear typed validation and policy checks. The model may propose; it must not quietly decide. Tests That Make the Design Believable A contract test checks that a repeated start yields one instance. Send POST /v1/workflows/{type} twice with an identical idempotency key, then assert that both responses carry the same instance id. A failure-injection test runs the key drill: a fault after payment has gone through. charge(...) succeeds; the CRM update then fails permanently. The workflow should refund. Replaying from history should then find the payment already made and skip the charge. A true crash-and-resume test, which kills the worker between the two steps, works the same way: replay reads history, skips the charge and picks up at the first step not yet done. The rule behind both: the durable history and the completion receipt decide whether to redeliver or compensate; worker memory never does. import pytest @pytest.mark.asyncio async def test_start_workflow_is_idempotent(client): payload = { "workflow_type": "order_approval", "business_payload": {"order_id": "o-123", "amount_cents": 5000}, "correlation_id": "corr-1", } headers = {"Idempotency-Key": "start:o-123"} first = await client.post("/v1/workflows/order_approval", json=payload, headers=headers) second = await client.post("/v1/workflows/order_approval", json=payload, headers=headers) assert first.status_code == 201 assert second.status_code in (200, 201) assert second.json()["instance_id"] == first.json()["instance_id"] @pytest.mark.asyncio async def test_worker_crash_after_payment_does_not_double_charge(orchestrator, fake_activities): order = Order(id="o-123", amount_cents=5000, customer_email="a@example.com") async def approval(order_id, timeout_days): return True async def charge_succeeds(*args, **kwargs): return PaymentReceipt(idempotency_key="pay:o-123", external_ref="payref-1", status="captured") fake_activities.charge.side_effect = charge_succeeds fake_activities.update_crm.side_effect = PermanentError("crm unavailable") with pytest.raises(PermanentError): await order_workflow(order, fake_activities, approval) # On replay, the orchestrator should consult history/receipts and not charge again. await orchestrator.replay_from_history(order.id) assert fake_activities.charge.await_count == 1 assert fake_activities.refund.await_count == 1 Together they prove that the API contract is idempotent in practice, and that the most important drill in this design holds: a failure after a successful payment ends in a refund, and replay never charges twice. Why This Answer Sounds Credible in an Interview Weak answer: "We'll add retries, and that makes it reliable." Strong answer: workflow state belongs to the orchestrator. Each side effect carries an idempotency key. Each state transition is versioned. Each replay is driven by history. Compensation is spelled out, never implied. With those parts made concrete, the rest of the system can be explained rather than taken on faith.

    • Timer(instance_id, fire_at): a record of each scheduled wake-up.
      • Purpose: wake a workflow after a long wait, expire an approval, or check whether an outside job has finished.
      • Primary key: (instance_id, fire_at), or whatever key the scheduler uses instead.

  • Ownership is split. The orchestrator holds workflow state, the history of steps and the intent to retry. Payments, document approval, email delivery and CRM (customer relationship management) updates belong to external systems. The orchestrator may record a payment, but it never acts as the financial ledger.
API Contracts
  • Four API contracts expose the state machine. Each is quick to explain, yet strict enough that no client can slip vague work into the engine:
    • POST /v1/workflows/{type}: begins a new workflow.
      • Authentication: normal caller authentication, scoped to the tenant or customer.
      • Idempotency: the caller sends an idempotency key, so a retried call never yields a second instance.
      • Request: the workflow type, the business payload, caller context and, if wanted, correlation metadata.
      • Response: the instance id, the starting state and a status reference that does not change.
      • Errors: 400 for a malformed request; 401/403 when auth fails; 409 while a request with that key is still in flight; 422 when the key returns with a different payload, or the inputs make no business sense. This split of 409 and 422 comes from the IETF Idempotency-Key draft, which had expired by Sep 2026: an Internet-Draft, not an RFC.
    • POST /v1/workflows/{id}/signals: accepts input from a person or another system.
      • Authentication: the caller needs permission to signal this workflow or tenant.
      • Idempotency: a signal id combined with a payload hash, or a caller key, filters out double-clicked approvals and repeated system callbacks.
      • Response: the accepted signal and the transition it caused, or a no-op when that signal has already been applied.
    • GET /v1/workflows/{id}/history: returns the audit trail.
      • Authentication: the caller needs read rights for the workflow's tenant and policy scope.
      • Semantics: it never writes; results come back in pages, sorted by sequence.
      • Errors: 404 when the workflow does not exist; 403 when access policy hides it.
    • POST /v1/workflows/{id}/repair: gives operators, or automation they have approved, a way to resume, replay or compensate.
      • Authentication: elevated operator authorisation with a narrow scope.
      • Idempotency: each repair action carries its own idempotency token. An operator who clicks twice should not cause twice the side effects.
      • Semantics: the call must state plainly which action it takes: retry a step, compensate a finished step, or resume from a known checkpoint.
  • Duplicates should behave predictably. If the payment step sees one idempotency key twice, the first call takes the money and saves a receipt. The second returns that receipt, or a "completed already" response.
The Implementation Slice That Proves the Design
  • One saga step is enough to show the key behaviour: wait for approval, take payment idempotently, update the CRM, and compensate if a downstream step fails for good.
  • The sketch is narrow by design. Production code would also need a scheduler, queue workers, persistence, serialisation, distributed locking and stronger typing. Here we keep only the state transitions an interviewer cares about most.
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Protocol


class PermanentError(Exception):
    pass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Order:
    id: str
    amount_cents: int
    customer_email: str


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class PaymentReceipt:
    idempotency_key: str
    external_ref: str
    status: str


class Activities(Protocol):
    async def charge(self, order: Order, idempotency_key: str) -> PaymentReceipt: ...
    async def update_crm(self, order: Order, idempotency_key: str) -> None: ...
    async def send_receipt(self, order: Order, idempotency_key: str) -> None: ...
    async def refund(self, payment: PaymentReceipt, idempotency_key: str) -> None: ...


async def order_workflow(order: Order, activities: Activities, wait_for_approval):
    if order.amount_cents <= 0:
        raise ValueError("order amount must be positive")

    approved = await wait_for_approval(order.id, timeout_days=7)
    if not approved:
        return "rejected"

    payment_key = f"pay:{order.id}"
    payment = await activities.charge(order, idempotency_key=payment_key)

    try:
        await activities.update_crm(order, idempotency_key=f"crm:{order.id}")
        await activities.send_receipt(order, idempotency_key=f"mail:{order.id}")
    except PermanentError:
        await activities.refund(payment, idempotency_key=f"refund:{order.id}")
        raise

    return "completed"
  • What each part does, in an order you can talk through out loud:
    • Order and PaymentReceipt are typed objects at the boundary. They stop the orchestration code from passing loose blobs around.
    • PermanentError separates failures worth a business retry from failures that should start compensation.
    • Activities is a protocol rather than a concrete dependency. That makes it easy to test, and it keeps vendor SDK details out of the workflow logic.
    • order_workflow(...) coordinates the saga.
    • The opening check turns away plainly bad input before any side effect. It is typed validation at the workflow's edge.
    • Waiting for approval creates a pause that must survive restarts. In production, a timer and stored state back it, not a bare function call.
    • payment_key = f"pay:{order.id}" guards the charge. A retry, a worker crash or a redelivered message cannot trigger a second one.
    • activities.charge(...) touches the outside world. The orchestrator reads its return value as a receipt; the payment ledger remains the source of truth.
    • After payment, the saga moves on to update_crm(...) and then send_receipt(...).
    • except PermanentError compensates by issuing a refund.
    • Raising the error again keeps the failure visible. The orchestrator can then record the terminal state and show it in history.

Interview pointer: Expect a question on how fine-grained the idempotency keys are, and answer it head-on. Each business action with a side effect gets its own key (pay:, crm:, mail:, refund:). The workflow as a whole does not share one. That single detail moves an answer from a whiteboard sketch to something a team could run in production.

What the Whiteboard Version Omits on Purpose
  • The short snippet leaves out concurrency control, versioning and observability hooks. A real build needs all of them:
    • Optimistic concurrency: each WorkflowInstance update checks a version number, so two workers cannot both move the same instance forward from stale state. In practice: "update where version = expected_version"; if another worker got there first, retry or abort.
    • Schema and contract versioning: definition_version on the instance lets old and new definitions run at the same time. An instance in flight stays on the version it began with, unless an explicit migration policy says otherwise.
    • Idempotency at every write boundary: payment is only one case. Repair actions, email sends, CRM updates and approval signals should be as safe to replay, where that is feasible.
    • Observability: every transition should produce metrics, trace spans and structured logs, tagged with step name, outcome and instance_id. The history table is the system of record. Telemetry is there for fast diagnosis.
    • Policy checks around model output: an LLM (large language model) might classify, route or summarise work inside a step. Before that output can change state or fire an external action, it must clear typed validation and policy checks. The model may propose; it must not quietly decide.
Tests That Make the Design Believable
  • A contract test checks that a repeated start yields one instance. Send POST /v1/workflows/{type} twice with an identical idempotency key, then assert that both responses carry the same instance id.
  • A failure-injection test runs the key drill: a fault after payment has gone through. charge(...) succeeds; the CRM update then fails permanently. The workflow should refund. Replaying from history should then find the payment already made and skip the charge. A true crash-and-resume test, which kills the worker between the two steps, works the same way: replay reads history, skips the charge and picks up at the first step not yet done. The rule behind both: the durable history and the completion receipt decide whether to redeliver or compensate; worker memory never does.

    payload = {
        "workflow_type": "order_approval",
        "business_payload": {"order_id": "o-123", "amount_cents": 5000},
        "correlation_id": "corr-1",
    }
    headers = {"Idempotency-Key": "start:o-123"}

    first = await client.post("/v1/workflows/order_approval", json=payload, headers=headers)
    second = await client.post("/v1/workflows/order_approval", json=payload, headers=headers)

    assert first.status_code == 201
    assert second.status_code in (200, 201)
    assert second.json()["instance_id"] == first.json()["instance_id"]


@pytest.mark.asyncio

    order = Order(id="o-123", amount_cents=5000, customer_email="a@example.com")
    async def approval(order_id, timeout_days):
        return True

    async def charge_succeeds(*args, **kwargs):
        return PaymentReceipt(idempotency_key="pay:o-123", external_ref="payref-1", status="captured")

    fake_activities.charge.side_effect = charge_succeeds
    fake_activities.update_crm.side_effect = PermanentError("crm unavailable")

    await orchestrator.replay_from_history(order.id)

  • Together they prove that the API contract is idempotent in practice, and that the most important drill in this design holds: a failure after a successful payment ends in a refund, and replay never charges twice.
Why This Answer Sounds Credible in an Interview

  • Strong answer: workflow state belongs to the orchestrator. Each side effect carries an idempotency key. Each state transition is versioned. Each replay is driven by history. Compensation is spelled out, never implied.
  • With those parts made concrete, the rest of the system can be explained rather than taken on faith.

sections.text: 6. Security, Reliability, and Failure HandlingThe Uncomfortable Question That Anchors This Section Picture the design review. Security, operations and the customer's admin are all in the room, and within minutes someone asks the hard one: the payment went through, then the worker died. Now what? That one injected fault teaches more than twelve questions about the happy path. It shows where the system's real edges lie. Think about what the orchestration layer protects: money movement, approval state, messages to customers and the integrations further downstream. It must keep each of them safe from half-finished runs, replays, operator mistakes and hostile access. A design that fails this drill is a best-effort script with a database behind it. Threat Model Before Failure Policy The design rests on four security controls: Authorise starts, signals, and repairs at the correct strength. Anyone who starts a workflow needs at least the permission required to read the customer object that workflow will change. Each signal (approval, rejection, resubmission, cancellation, override) must carry authentication, be limited to the right tenant and workflow instance, and pass a check against the current state machine. Repairs need the tightest control of all, because they can skip the normal sequence and change a business effect after it has already happened. Keep secrets out of history. History is how the system remembers, which also makes it a target. A token, API key, password or full payment artifact stored there can be replayed or exported. It can also be shown to operators who need to see state but have no reason to see credentials. The safer pattern keeps only opaque references in history. At execution time the worker pulls a short-lived secret from a secret manager or a KMS-backed vault, with the narrowest scope and a clear expiry. Restrict operator mutation paths. An operator's job is to pause, inspect and resume. It is not to rewrite state transitions at will, or to quietly record money as collected. Any manual change goes through a narrow repair API that validates input, checks versions and logs the approval. This is defence in depth: authenticated admin access, permission checks based on role, immutable audit logs and state-machine rules each guard one boundary from a different side. Audit every compensation and manual override. Reversed payments, voided document approvals and hand-repaired CRM (customer relationship management) records must all leave a trail. Record who started the action, the reason, the instance it touched and the state version it aimed at. With that evidence, the post-incident review rests on facts rather than guesses. Failure Policies Are Design Decisions, Not Afterthoughts In the interview, say out loud which branches fail open, which fail closed, which degrade, which queue and which need a person. Using those words with care is itself a sign of judgement. Here is where the common branches land: Fail closed: approval completion, payment authorisation, repair mutations, and any step that could record a business effect that never happened. Degrade: if the customer is happy with eventual delivery, email can fall back to queued sending or a later notice. Queue: CRM sync, internal analytics updates and noncritical enrichment can wait in line while a transient outage clears. Human intervention: approvals that are unclear, poison messages that keep failing, and policy exceptions that code cannot settle safely. Fail open only with extreme caution: occasionally acceptable for a read-only status view; never acceptable for an external side effect that cannot be undone. Treat blast radius as a working control. Partition every retry queue, dead-letter stream and repair lane by tenant, region, workflow type and dependency. Then a stuck CRM connector cannot block document approvals for tenants it has nothing to do with. Likewise, a regional outage must not quietly spill over a region line unless both the customer contract and the data policy say it may. Failure Drill: Worker Crashes After Payment Succeeds Detection: the lease expires, heartbeats stop arriving, or the orchestrator's own timeout fires. Containment: never send the charge a second time. Recovery: replay the history, see that the charge step finished, and pick up at the first step that has not. Prevention: put an idempotency key on the payment request. Keep a durable history that writes the intent before the call and the completion once the acknowledgement arrives. Of all the incident drills, this one matters most. Security and operations inject the crash. The candidate has to show how the system limits the damage and keeps the evidence intact, not how they would scramble to get things running again. Interview pointer: If you are asked what happens when the worker dies after the payment goes through, build the answer on one sentence: the durable history and the completion receipt decide whether to redeliver or compensate; worker memory never does. A lost worker is not a lost business action. Tie detection, containment, recovery and prevention back to durable history every time. Failure Drill: Email Succeeds but CRM Fails Detection: track side effects per step rather than per job. The email worker may report success while the CRM update times out or comes back with a permanent error. Containment: rather than pretend the whole process worked, the workflow moves into a state that can be compensated or repaired. Recovery: retry the CRM call idempotently, hand the item off to dead-letter handling, or open a manual reconciliation task when a person must validate the CRM record. Prevention: keep a status for each step and carry explicit correlation IDs. Set a policy that workflow state is authoritative and notifications are not. Failure Drill: Approval Waits Seven Days In orchestration, a long wait is ordinary, not exceptional. The system has to provide durable timers, state that people can see, and a way to deal with stale instances. Detection: this raises no failure alarm. A timeout threshold routes the instance to the queue that should act on it. Containment: do not burn worker capacity on polling that never ends. Recovery: depending on policy, send the reminder again, escalate to a manager, or let the request expire. Prevention/design intent: waiting is a first-class state in the workflow, not a sleep loop improvised for the occasion. Failure Drill: Definition Changes While Instances Run Treat this as a versioning problem, not only a deployment concern. Detection: the runtime notices that the definition hash or version does not match. Containment: each old instance keeps running on the version it began with, unless someone has defined an explicit migration path. Recovery: either route steps by version so old instances stay forward compatible, or run a controlled migration that is tested and audited. Prevention: each durable instance stores its definition version. Each new deployment either publishes a compatible contract or declares a deliberate break. Failure Drill: External API Times Out Indefinitely Four things are needed here: timeouts with a bound, retries that back off, a circuit breaker, and a route to dead-letter handling or escalation. Detection: no progress inside a known limit. Containment: stop pounding the dependency, and shield the worker pool. Recovery: a scheduled retry, a fallback queue, or a person stepping in when the downstream system stays down for a long stretch. Prevention: put a time bound on every call to a dependency. Have the orchestration policy treat transient and permanent failures differently. Evidence the Interviewers Want to Hear Before go-live, you should be able to walk through the audit evidence and the runbooks. Who may start a workflow? How does someone ask for a repair, and who signs it off? Where do compensation logs live? How does support get a replay explained to them? How do you prove that a crash did not lead to a duplicate payment? Make that evidence searchable by tenant and workflow id. Keep it for as long as the customer's policy and jurisdictional rules require. For observability, trace each transition with correlation ids. Emit counters for retries, compensations, dead-letter items and manual overrides. Raise an alert when the counts of requested, completed and compensated steps drift apart. Beyond knowing that something is broken, you want to know which tenant, which dependency and which failure policy is soaking up the impact right now. Interview-Sized Code Sketch: No-Double-Charge Invariant The test is narrow: crash the workflow at the worst moment, and replay must still not repeat an irreversible side effect. Treat this as a teaching sketch sized for an interview. It leaves out persistence details, dependency wiring and the full workflow engine. A production build would put the event log on durable storage, add validation and pin library versions. import pytest class FakePayments: def __init__(self): self._charges = {} def charge(self, order_id: str) -> str: self._charges[order_id] = self._charges.get(order_id, 0) + 1 return f"charge-{order_id}" def charge_count(self, order_id: str) -> int: return self._charges.get(order_id, 0) class CrashAfterCharge(Exception): pass class WorkflowEngine: def __init__(self, payments: FakePayments): self.payments = payments self.history = [] self.completed = set() async def run_until_crash(self, order_id: str, crash_after: str | None = None): if "charge" not in self.completed: self.history.append(("intent", "charge", order_id)) self.payments.charge(order_id) self.history.append(("done", "charge", order_id)) self.completed.add("charge") if crash_after == "charge": raise CrashAfterCharge() async def resume_workflow(self, order_id: str): if "charge" not in self.completed: self.history.append(("resume", "charge", order_id)) self.payments.charge(order_id) self.history.append(("done", "charge", order_id)) self.completed.add("charge") self.history.append(("next", "crm", order_id)) @pytest.mark.asyncio async def test_crash_after_payment_does_not_charge_twice(): payments = FakePayments() engine = WorkflowEngine(payments) order_id = "order-123" with pytest.raises(CrashAfterCharge): await engine.run_until_crash(order_id, crash_after="charge") await engine.resume_workflow(order_id) assert payments.charge_count(order_id) == 1 The workflow has to keep enough state to tell "attempted" apart from "completed". Recovery must check that state before it decides to repeat the side effect. A production version would also validate arguments, persist state, log in a structured format, handle timeouts, and pass an explicit idempotency key through to the payment gateway request. What to Say When the Interviewer Pushes on Trade-offs Customer wants faster recovery → automate more of the compensations, and accept a higher chance that an automated undo gets it wrong. Business wants stronger correctness → fail closed more often, and accept deeper queues and more work for people. Platform has to serve many tenants → draw sharper blast-radius boundaries and tighten operator permissions. An FDE (Forward Deployed Engineer) is accountable for safe rollout, support and incident response as well as the happy path. A good answer keeps the customer's business effect safe, holds on to evidence for the postmortem, and still pushes the workflow forward without repeating any irreversible action.

  • Containment: each old instance keeps running on the version it began with, unless someone has defined an explicit migration path.
  • Recovery: either route steps by version so old instances stay forward compatible, or run a controlled migration that is tested and audited.
  • Prevention: each durable instance stores its definition version. Each new deployment either publishes a compatible contract or declares a deliberate break.
Failure Drill: External API Times Out Indefinitely
  • Four things are needed here: timeouts with a bound, retries that back off, a circuit breaker, and a route to dead-letter handling or escalation.
  • Detection: no progress inside a known limit.
  • Containment: stop pounding the dependency, and shield the worker pool.
  • Recovery: a scheduled retry, a fallback queue, or a person stepping in when the downstream system stays down for a long stretch.
  • Prevention: put a time bound on every call to a dependency. Have the orchestration policy treat transient and permanent failures differently.

  • Before go-live, you should be able to walk through the audit evidence and the runbooks. Who may start a workflow? How does someone ask for a repair, and who signs it off?   • Make that evidence searchable by tenant and workflow id. Keep it for as long as the customer's policy and jurisdictional rules require.
  • For observability, trace each transition with correlation ids. Emit counters for retries, compensations, dead-letter items and manual overrides. Raise an alert when the counts of requested, completed and compensated steps drift apart.
  • Beyond knowing that something is broken, you want to know which tenant, which dependency and which failure policy is soaking up the impact right now.
Interview-Sized Code Sketch: No-Double-Charge Invariant
  • The test is narrow: crash the workflow at the worst moment, and replay must still not repeat an irreversible side effect.

import pytest


class FakePayments:
    def __init__(self):
        self._charges = {}

    def charge(self, order_id: str) -> str:
        self._charges[order_id] = self._charges.get(order_id, 0) + 1
        return f"charge-{order_id}"

    def charge_count(self, order_id: str) -> int:
        return self._charges.get(order_id, 0)


class CrashAfterCharge(Exception):
    pass


class WorkflowEngine:
    def __init__(self, payments: FakePayments):
        self.payments = payments
        self.history = []
        self.completed = set()

    async def run_until_crash(self, order_id: str, crash_after: str | None = None):
        if "charge" not in self.completed:
            self.history.append(("intent", "charge", order_id))
            self.payments.charge(order_id)
            self.history.append(("done", "charge", order_id))
            self.completed.add("charge")
            if crash_after == "charge":
                raise CrashAfterCharge()

    async def resume_workflow(self, order_id: str):
        if "charge" not in self.completed:
            self.history.append(("resume", "charge", order_id))
            self.payments.charge(order_id)
            self.history.append(("done", "charge", order_id))
            self.completed.add("charge")
        self.history.append(("next", "crm", order_id))


@pytest.mark.asyncio
async def test_crash_after_payment_does_not_charge_twice():
    payments = FakePayments()
    engine = WorkflowEngine(payments)
    order_id = "order-123"

    with pytest.raises(CrashAfterCharge):
        await engine.run_until_crash(order_id, crash_after="charge")

    await engine.resume_workflow(order_id)
    assert payments.charge_count(order_id) == 1
  • The workflow has to keep enough state to tell "attempted" apart from "completed". Recovery must check that state before it decides to repeat the side effect.
  • A production version would also validate arguments, persist state, log in a structured format, handle timeouts, and pass an explicit idempotency key through to the payment gateway request.
What to Say When the Interviewer Pushes on Trade-offs
  • Customer wants faster recovery → automate more of the compensations, and accept a higher chance that an automated undo gets it wrong.
  • Business wants stronger correctness → fail closed more often, and accept deeper queues and more work for people.
  • Platform has to serve many tenants → draw sharper blast-radius boundaries and tighten operator permissions.
  • An FDE (Forward Deployed Engineer) is accountable for safe rollout, support and incident response as well as the happy path. sections.text: 8. Interview Walkthrough, Trade-Offs, and PracticeMinute-Zero Opening: Lead with the Business Effect Sound like an FDE (Forward Deployed Engineer) who is already in the room with a customer under production pressure. Do not sound like a candidate listing patterns. Start from the outcome and flag the riskiest assumptions early. Then keep steering back to three things: the business effect, how the system recovers, and what control operators keep. Model opening: "Approval of documents, a payment, an email and three internal systems all have to move together, and any one of them can fail or sit waiting for days. My goal is to apply each business effect of a long-running process exactly once, keep its state visible, and compensate when a step fails. First I'll pin down what a successful business effect means here. Next I'll size the workflow volume. Then I'll propose the orchestration model, the storage and the recovery approach. I'll finish with failure handling, security and rollout." That opening earns four things in one go. It proves you grasp the customer's need, centres the design on business effect rather than plain task execution, and signals a plan for the hour. It also lets the interviewer steer you if their setting has a different constraint. A Practical 50-Minute Answer Plan Spend minutes where the risk is, not where the diagram is biggest: 0–5 min: discovery and assumptions. Find out what a finished workflow looks like. Ask which steps a person does and which are automated, whether an approval can take hours or days, and which system owns the truth about state. Say your assumptions aloud and ask to be corrected. 5–10 min: scope and scale. Estimate how many workflows are active, how long each runs on average and how many instances peak at once. Add the extra writes that history and retries create. Use that to choose between a simple queue-based engine and a sturdier, durable workflow service. 10–20 min: architecture. Sketch the orchestration boundary, the workflow state store, the worker pool, idempotent activity executors, compensation handlers and the external systems. Make clear that the orchestrator owns ordering and durable state, while workers carry out the side effects. 20–28 min: failure modes. Step through four cases: a worker crashing after payment, a timeout while approval is pending, a webhook delivered twice, and a run that completes only partly across internal systems. For each, explain which guard stops the duplicate: the event history, the retry policy, the idempotency keys, or a compensation or escalation path. 28–35 min: security and controls. Walk through who the caller is at each hop (identity propagation), least privilege, secret handling, audit logs, retention, and what you redact or minimise. Each control should answer a named failure mode or compliance need. 35–42 min: product and operations. Talk through observability, dashboards for operators, how stuck workflows get handled and how in-flight workflows are versioned. Show that one platform can serve many business processes, so it does not turn into a factory for one-off scripts. 42–47 min: trade-offs and alternatives. Weigh an orchestrated saga against choreography, history size against debuggability, automatic compensation against human review, and workflow code against declarative definitions. 47–50 min: close with a concise executive summary. Come back to the customer outcome, the architecture, the largest trade-off and the gate for rollout. Keeping the Conversation at the Right Depth Candidates often lose the hour drawing boxes and leave the fragile edges almost untouched. Let the risk profile set how deep you go: Approvals that can wait a week → long-lived state and versioning outweigh small latency optimisations. Payments that cannot be undone → idempotency and compensation outweigh clever orchestration syntax. Several internal systems that are only eventually consistent → event ordering and reconciliation outweigh the precise choice of queue. Minute-Zero Opening: Lead with the Business Effect

Start from the outcome and flag the riskiest assumptions early. Then keep steering back to three things: the business effect, how the system recovers, and what control operators keep.
  • Model opening: "Approval of documents, a payment, an email and three internal systems all have to move together, and any one of them can fail or sit waiting for days. My goal is to apply each business effect of a long-running process exactly once, keep its state visible, and compensate when a step fails. First I'll pin down what a successful business effect means here. Next I'll size the workflow volume. Then I'll propose the orchestration model, the storage and the recovery approach. I'll finish with failure handling, security and rollout."
  • That opening earns four things in one go. It proves you grasp the customer's need, centres the design on business effect rather than plain task execution, and signals a plan for the hour. It also lets the interviewer steer you if their setting has a different constraint.
A Practical 50-Minute Answer Plan
  • Spend minutes where the risk is, not where the diagram is biggest:
    • 0–5 min: discovery and assumptions. Find out what a finished workflow looks like. Ask which steps a person does and which are automated, whether an approval can take hours or days, and which system owns the truth about state. Say your assumptions aloud and ask to be corrected.
    • 5–10 min: scope and scale. Estimate how many workflows are active, how long each runs on average and how many instances peak at once. Add the extra writes that history and retries create. Use that to choose between a simple queue-based engine and a sturdier, durable workflow service.
    • 10–20 min: architecture. Sketch the orchestration boundary, the workflow state store, the worker pool, idempotent activity executors, compensation handlers and the external systems. Make clear that the orchestrator owns ordering and durable state, while workers carry out the side effects.
    • 20–28 min: failure modes.     • 28–35 min: security and controls. Walk through who the caller is at each hop (identity propagation), least privilege, secret handling, audit logs, retention, and what you redact or minimise. Each control should answer a named failure mode or compliance need.
    • 35–42 min: product and operations. Talk through observability, dashboards for operators, how stuck workflows get handled and how in-flight workflows are versioned. Show that one platform can serve many business processes, so it does not turn into a factory for one-off scripts.
    • 42–47 min: trade-offs and alternatives. Weigh an orchestrated saga against choreography, history size against debuggability, automatic compensation against human review, and workflow code against declarative definitions.

    • Approvals that can wait a week → long-lived state and versioning outweigh small latency optimisations.
    • Payments that cannot be undone → idempotency and compensation outweigh clever orchestration syntax.

  • History size vs. debuggability.
    • Keeping every transition, input, output and retry helps debugging, because you can replay the path a decision took and see exactly where it failed. The price is growing storage, heavier reads and more care with redaction.

  • Architecture: Was there a clean account of control flow, durable state, how workers behave and the external integrations?
  • Depth: Did crash recovery, idempotency and versioning get more time than drawing boxes?
  • Security: Were least privilege, secret handling, audit trails and keeping data to a minimum all raised?
  • Delivery: Were rollout, tools for operators and the handoff to support covered?

The formula: cost per workflow ≈ infra marginal cost + (manual repair rate × loaded operator cost per incident). Both inputs come from SLIs we already track: compensation rate and manual repair count. So I'd say, "We already have the inputs. We just haven't multiplied them yet." No new metric is needed. Managed durable-execution products already do that job well. For most teams the sensible default is to buy the execution runtime and build the workflow definitions and activities. Spend build effort only where we differ from everyone else. A rule worth saying out loud: buy the commodity execution layer, and let the vendor answer for keeping it durable and up. Build only the business state machine and the policy layer, because no vendor can get those right for you. Item 17: going deeper on regulation and governance (Partial). I'd name the frameworks an interviewer is probably fishing for and pin each one to a part we already built. First, PCI-DSS. If the orchestrator would ever handle card data, push that data to the payment gateway and hold only opaque references. This matches the "keep secrets out of history" control in Section 6 and shrinks PCI scope. Second, SOX-style controls, if an approval counts as a financial authorisation. The ActivityReceipt record and the audit-log fields in Section 5 already give a SOX auditor the evidence trail they would request. Third, GDPR and data minimisation, if an internal system handles customer PII (personally identifiable information). We would enforce it through the retention policy that Section 5 sets on HistoryEvent. I'd frame governance as rules on records we already keep, rather than a new stream of work. Our design touches AI in one place: before an LLM-driven step changes state, it must pass "typed validation and policy checks" (Section 5). I'd take that further with a concrete case. Suppose an LLM misreads or misroutes an approval. It could quietly approve something a human should have seen. That is an irreversible business effect, the same kind the failure-policy table in Section 6 already tells us to fail closed on. So responsible AI needs no new framework. It plugs into the decision table we already have. Treat any model output that could start a payment, finish an approval or trigger a repair as untrusted input. Route it through the same human-review lane we already keep for irreversible or ambiguous compensation.

  • Both inputs come from SLIs we already track: compensation rate and manual repair count. So I'd say, "We already have the inputs. We just haven't multiplied them yet." No new metric is needed.

Item 10: building, buying and picking vendors or models (Absent).

  • I'd state it plainly. The state machine, the history store and the replay engine form the durable-execution core. Managed durable-execution products already do that job well. For most teams the sensible default is to buy the execution runtime and build the workflow definitions and activities.
  • Spend build effort only where we differ from everyone else. That means three things: the compensation policy for each business action (the fail-closed, degrade, queue and human-intervention table in Section 6), where each idempotency key's boundary sits (Section 5), and the saga logic for our domain, which is the order_workflow function itself.
  • A rule worth saying out loud: buy the commodity execution layer, and let the vendor answer for keeping it durable and up. Build only the business state machine and the policy layer, because no vendor can get those right for you.

Item 17: going deeper on regulation and governance (Partial).

  • I'd name the frameworks an interviewer is probably fishing for and pin each one to a part we already built. First, PCI-DSS. If the orchestrator would ever handle card data, push that data to the payment gateway and hold only opaque references. This matches the "keep secrets out of history" control in Section 6 and shrinks PCI scope.
  • Second, SOX-style controls, if an approval counts as a financial authorisation. The ActivityReceipt record and the audit-log fields in Section 5 already give a SOX auditor the evidence trail they would request.
  • Third, GDPR and data minimisation, if an internal system handles customer PII (personally identifiable information). We would enforce it through the retention policy that Section 5 sets on HistoryEvent. I'd frame governance as rules on records we already keep, rather than a new stream of work.

Item 18: responsible AI, past the failure everyone expects (Partial).

  • Our design touches AI in one place: before an LLM-driven step changes state, it must pass "typed validation and policy checks" (Section 5). I'd take that further with a concrete case. Suppose an LLM misreads or misroutes an approval. It could quietly approve something a human should have seen. That is an irreversible business effect, the same kind the failure-policy table in Section 6 already tells us to fail closed on.
  • So responsible AI needs no new framework. It plugs into the decision table we already have. Treat any model output that could start a payment, finish an approval or trigger a repair as untrusted input. Route it through the same human-review lane we already keep for irreversible or ambiguous compensation.

Sarbanes-Oxley Act: The US law on financial-reporting controls. It is why finance teams want every change to leave an audit trail.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
sections.text: Key Takeaways State the goal as one outcome: apply each business effect of a long-running process exactly once, keep its state visible, and compensate when a step fails. Treat payment as the riskiest step because it cannot be reversed, so whatever else degrades, the design must still block a second payment. Size from 10 million active workflows and 100 million activities a day, about 1,157 activities a second on average, then plan for peaks of 3x to 10x with at least double the observed peak as headroom. Keep workflow state small and park documents and payloads in object storage, so 40 events of 1 KB across 10 million workflows stay near 400 GB of raw history. At 10x growth, 1 billion activities a day or about 11.6k a second, expect replay latency, queue hot spots, storage fan-out or cost to break before application-server CPU does. Split the control plane (registry, scheduler, timers, signal gateway, compensation engine, operations UI) from the data plane (queues and workers), so decisions scale apart from side effects. Only the durable history store owns workflow progress: queues handle delivery, workers suggest effects, and the scheduler rebuilds its view from history each time. Pin each running instance to the definition version it started with, and ship changes as a new version instead of editing executions in flight. Make deterministic replay and crash recovery the first rollout gate, ahead of operator visibility and migration by version. Prefer an orchestrated saga over choreography, because choreography lowers coupling but then nobody can point to where a run stands.

sections.text: Strong functional requirements Core workflow: one process has to span payment, email, document approval and three internal systems, and its business effect must land exactly once. Model waiting as a proper state that timers and signals drive. While a person decides, no worker sleeps in a loop. Pair each step with an action that undoes its effect. Partial failure then leaves something repairable, never a silent half-success. Put a version on every workflow definition. An instance finishes on the version it began with. Operators need to resume, replay or compensate a single named instance, and each of those actions goes into the audit trail.
