sections.title: Architecture explanation
sections.text: Architecture explanation Deciding what happens next is the control plane's job. Its parts are the definition registry, the scheduler, the timer service, the signal gateway, the compensation engine and the operations UI. Doing the work is the data plane's job. Its queues and workers make the calls to payment, email, the CRM (customer relationship management) and the internal systems. Only the start call runs synchronously. It validates input, authenticates the caller, checks permissions, appends the first history event and hands back the workflow ID. All later work is asynchronous. That covers dispatching activities, waiting on approvals, waking on timers, retrying and compensating. Ownership splits cleanly. Workflow state, the step history and the intent to retry belong to the orchestrator. External systems own the rest: CRM records, the payment itself, email delivery and document approval. History only grows. Before a step runs, it records the intent; once the external system acknowledges, it records completion. Because of that order, replaying after a crash is safe. A deadline wakes an instance through the timer service, and a human action wakes it through the signal gateway. So a wait of seven days ties up no worker. Each instance row uses optimistic concurrency. Two workers holding stale state cannot both advance it.

sections.title: Data model / integration assumptions
sections.text: Data model / integration assumptions Core records: WorkflowInstance carries id, state, definition_version and next_event. HistoryEvent carries instance_id, sequence, type and payload_ref. ActivityReceipt carries idempotency_key, external_ref and status. Timer carries instance_id and fire_at. Nobody edits a HistoryEvent once written. When a workflow crashes, replaying those events tells it what has already been done. An ActivityReceipt exists for every external side effect. A repeat of the same idempotency key gets the saved receipt back, and the card is not charged again. Every instance keeps the definition version it started on. Deploying mid-run therefore cannot silently swap the rules under it. Documents live in external storage, and payload_ref is a pointer to them. That keeps state small and replay cheap.

sections.title: Rollout plan
sections.text: Rollout plan Week 0-1: pick a single workflow; do not build a platform. Record what we assume about payment idempotency and how long waits may last. Week 1-2: gate one is determinism plus crash recovery. Kill a worker mid-run and demonstrate the instance resuming from its history. sections.title: Final 2-minute spoken answer
sections.text: Final 2-minute spoken answerI'd hold off on choosing an engine. We're asked to make payment, email, three internal systems and document approval work as one process, and any step in it may fail or stall for days. The tempting summary is "build an orchestrator that calls these APIs." That's only wiring. A better summary starts from the outcome. Long business processes must apply each business effect exactly once, show their state, and compensate when a step fails. Framed like that, the requirements fall out at once: idempotency, durable state, retries, pauses for human approval, an audit trail and compensating actions. The thing we're guarding is a single business transaction stretched over days, not messages crossing a network. For the architecture, the control plane has the definition registry, the scheduler, the timer service, the signal gateway, the compensation engine and the operations UI. The data plane is queues plus workers, and those workers call payment, the CRM and email. Only the start is synchronous. It authenticates, authorises, appends the first history event and returns the ID. The rest runs asynchronously. History only grows: intent goes in before a step, completion goes in after the acknowledgement. The key drill shows why that matters. Say a worker dies just after the payment succeeds. We don't charge again. We replay history, find the completed charge, and continue at the next step still open. Waiting seven days for approval is a timer state; nothing polls. Each instance keeps its definition version, so a deployment can't alter its rules partway. My first move is one workflow. It goes live only after crash recovery works and duplicate effects are zero, and operators get visibility before we widen scope.
